spanish-basics.title: Spanish A1 — Foundations for Study & Immigration
spanish-basics.summary: Master Spanish A1 essentials: greetings, verb conjugation, gender/articles, and practical phrases for study and immigration purposes.

slides.title: Welcome to Spanish A1
points: Spanish A1 is the absolute beginner level — foundation for all future learning
Required for DELE A1, SIELE, and many immigration/study programs
Focus: essential survival phrases, basic grammar, everyday vocabulary
Goal: hold simple conversations, introduce yourself, ask for help

slides.title: Greetings & Introductions
points: Hola (hello), Buenos días (good morning), Buenas tardes (good afternoon), Buenas noches (good evening)
Me llamo... (My name is...), ¿Cómo te llamas? (What's your name?)
Mucho gusto (pleased to meet you), Encantado/a (delighted)
¿Cómo estás? (How are you?) → Estoy bien/mal/así así (I'm well/bad/so-so)

slides.title: Where Are You From?
points: Soy de... (I'm from...) + country: España, México, Argentina, Colombia
¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?)
Soy español/a, mexicano/a, argentino/a (nationality adjectives must agree with gender)
Vivo en... (I live in...) + city — Vivo en Madrid, Barcelona, Lima, etc.

slides.title: Ser vs. Estar — The Critical Distinction
points: SER (permanent identity): Soy ingeniero (I'm an engineer), Eres joven (You're young), Es mexicano (He's Mexican)
ESTAR (location/condition): Estoy en Madrid (I'm in Madrid), Estás cansado (You're tired), Está enfermo (He's sick)
SER: profession, nationality, characteristics; ESTAR: where/how you are now
Most common beginner mistake — confusing these two; master early to build confidence

slides.title: Ser Conjugation (Present)
points: Yo soy (I am), Tú eres (you are informal), Él/Ella/Usted es (he/she/you formal)
Nosotros/as somos (we are), Vosotros/as sois (you all — Spain only), Ellos/Ellas/Ustedes son (they/you all)
Memorize as a block: soy-eres-es-somos-sois-son
Repetition and writing: practice conjugating 5 min daily for one week

slides.title: Estar Conjugation (Present)
points: Yo estoy, Tú estás, Él/Ella/Usted está, Nosotros/as estamos, Vosotros/as estáis, Ellos/Ellas/Ustedes están
Pattern: est- + a, ás, á, amos, áis, án
Common locations: en la casa (at home), en el trabajo (at work), en la escuela (at school)
Practice: 'Yo estoy en Madrid' = location; 'Yo estoy cansado' = condition

slides.title: Gender & Articles (El/La/Los/Las)
points: El (masculine singular): el libro (the book), el gato (the cat)
La (feminine singular): la casa (the house), la gata (the cat fem.)
Los (masculine plural): los libros, Los gatos
Las (feminine plural): las casas, las gatas
Rule: -o endings usually masculine (el libro), -a endings usually feminine (la casa); exceptions exist

slides.title: Gender Practice: Common Nouns
points: Masculine: el libro, el café, el agua (!), el día, el hombre, el niño, el amigo
Feminine: la casa, la puerta, la mujer, la niña, la amiga, la mesa, la calle
Watch: 'agua' is feminine (el agua) — gender by first letter sound, not spelling
Plurals: add -s (libro→libros), or -es if ends in consonant (ciudad→ciudades)

slides.title: Numbers 0-100 & Time
points: 0-10: cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez
11-20: once, doce, trece, catorce, quince, dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve, veinte
21-30: veintiuno, veintidós, ..., treinta (then treinta y uno, treinta y dos, etc.)
Multiples: cuarenta (40), cincuenta (50), sesenta (60), setenta (70), ochenta (80), noventa (90), cien(to) (100)

slides.title: Telling Time & Days of the Week
points: ¿Qué hora es? (What time is it?) → Es la una (1:00), Son las dos (2:00), etc.
Use 'es' for 1:00, 'son' for all others; add y minutos for 15/30/45: Son las tres y cuarto (3:15)
Days: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo (not capitalized)
Months: enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre

slides.title: Essential Phrases for Immigration & Study
points: ¿Habla inglés? (Do you speak English?) → Sí, un poco (Yes, a little)
No entiendo (I don't understand) → ¿Puede repetir, por favor? (Can you repeat, please?)
¿Cuál es su visa? (What is your visa status?) → Visa de estudiante (Student visa)
Necesito... (I need...) documentos, ayuda, información (documents, help, information)

slides.title: School & Study Vocabulary
points: La escuela (school), La universidad (university), El estudiante/la estudiante (student), El profesor/la profesora (teacher)
El libro (book), El cuaderno (notebook), El lápiz (pencil), La tarea (homework), El examen (exam/test)
Voy a la escuela (I go to school) → future with 'ir + a + infinitive'
Estudio... medicina, ingeniería, negocios, idiomas (I study... medicine, engineering, business, languages)

slides.title: Family & Relationships
points: La familia (family): padre (father), madre (mother), hermano/hermana (brother/sister), abuelo/abuela (grandfather/grandmother)
Hijo/hija (son/daughter), tío/tía (uncle/aunt), primo/prima (cousin), esposo/esposa (husband/wife)
Tengo... (I have...) → Tengo un hermano (I have one brother), Tengo dos hermanas (I have two sisters)
¿Tienes familia en España? (Do you have family in Spain?) → Sí, tengo padres y un hermano

slides.title: Food & Drinks (Daily Survival)
points: Pan (bread), Agua (water), Café (coffee), Leche (milk), Arroz (rice), Pollo (chicken), Carne (meat), Verduras (vegetables)
Tengo hambre (I'm hungry), Tengo sed (I'm thirsty)
¿Qué deseas comer? (What would you like to eat?) → Quiero... (I want...) arroz con pollo
Gracias (thank you), De nada (you're welcome), Por favor (please)

slides.title: Regular Verb Conjugation (Present) — -AR, -ER, -IR
points: -AR (hablar): yo hablo, tú hablas, él habla, nosotros hablamos, vosotros habláis, ellos hablan
-ER (comer): yo como, tú comes, él come, nosotros comemos, ellos comen
-IR (vivir): yo vivo, tú vives, él vive, nosotros vivimos, ellos viven
Most A1 verbs are regular — master these patterns, and 80% of conversations become possible

slides.title: DELE A1 & SIELE Overview
points: DELE (Diploma de Español como Lengua Extranjera) A1: 3 papers (Reading, Writing, Listening), ~2.5 hours
SIELE (Servicio Internacional de Evaluación de la Lengua Española): computer-based, 4 parts (Reading, Listening, Writing, Speaking)
A1 tests: survival phrases, basic introductions, simple conversations, reading short texts
Both required for study/work visas in Spain and Latin America; DELE is older/more respected globally

slides.title: Study Plan for A1 Mastery
points: Weeks 1-2: Ser/Estar, greetings, numbers, days — daily 30 min conversation with a tutor/partner
Weeks 3-4: Gender, articles, -AR/-ER/-IR verbs, family/food vocab — write 5 short sentences daily
Weeks 5-6: Combine all above in dialogues (introduce yourself, ask how others are, order food, say where you live)
Week 7: Review, take a mock DELE/SIELE A1 test, identify weak areas, drill final 2 weeks

slides.title: Why Spanish for Study & Immigration?
points: Spain (EU): universities, tech jobs, residency pathways all require A1-B1 Spanish
Latin America (Mexico, Colombia, Argentina, Chile): over 500M speakers, growing tech/education hubs, visas favor Spanish speakers
Cost: Spain EU visas cheaper than UK/US; Latin America tech salaries rising, cost of living lower
Dual path: study in Spanish-speaking country, network, build career, then move/stay with earned credentials

slides.title: Common A1 Mistakes & How to Avoid Them
points: Confusing ser/estar: drill with 100+ sentences; ser = identity, estar = location
Gender errors: write nouns WITH their article (el/la) every time — builds muscle memory
Verb conjugation: irregular verbs (ir, tener, hacer) are high-frequency — memorize by repetition, not logic
Pronunciation: Spanish is phonetic — practice with native speakers, YouTube, or Forvo app to lock in sounds early

slides.title: Next Steps: A1 → A2
points: After A1: move to past tense (pretérito, imperfecto) and conditional (would/could)
A2 adds: longer conversations, reading paragraphs, writing short emails, connecting ideas with 'porque' (because), 'aunque' (although)
Real-world milestone: after A1-A2, you can travel, work in entry-level jobs, join university classes as a prepared student
Timeline: A1 (6-8 weeks intensive), A2 (10-12 weeks), B1 (3-4 months) — then you're job-ready in most Spanish-speaking countries

slides.title: ser vs. estar: The Core Distinction
points: ser (to be): permanent identity, profession, nationality, time (Soy María, soy ingeniera, soy española)
estar (to be): location, temporary state, feelings, condition (Estoy en Madrid, estoy feliz, estoy cansado)
Conjugation differs: ser (soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son) vs. estar (estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están)
Many adjectives change meaning: ser aburrido (to be boring) vs. estar aburrido (to be bored)

example.label: ser vs. estar
example.text: Yo soy ingeniero y estoy en la oficina. | Ella es simpática pero está de mal humor hoy. | Nosotros somos amigos y estamos juntos.

slides.tip: Mistakes with ser/estar are the #1 Spanish A1 error—drill both daily until distinction is automatic.

slides.title: Gender & Article Agreement
points: Masculine/feminine: almost all nouns end in -o (masculino) or -a (feminina), plus exceptions
Definite articles: el, la, los, las (the) | Indefinite: un, una, unos, unas (a/an, some)
Adjectives must agree: la casa blanca (fem), los libros blancos (masc plural)
Common errors: el problema (masc despite -a), la mano (fem despite -o)—memorize exceptions

example.label: Agreement in context
example.text: un libro rojo (a red book) | unos profesores inteligentes (some intelligent professors) | las muchachas altas (the tall girls)

slides.tip: Learn nouns with their article from day one (el gato, not just 'gato')—it sticks faster than learning gender separately.

slides.title: Present Tense: -ar, -er, -ir Conjugation
points: -ar verbs (hablar): hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan
-er verbs (comer): como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen
-ir verbs (vivir): vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven
Regular verbs follow these patterns—irregular verbs (ir, ser, estar, tener) learned separately

example.label: Conjugation across groups
example.text: Yo hablo español. | Tú comes pan. | Nosotros vivimos en Madrid. | Ellos hablan inglés.

slides.tip: Master 5 regular verbs per group (hablar, trabajar, comprar, comer, beber, vivir, escribir)—conjugation drills pay off.

slides.title: Numbers & Price Negotiation
points: 0–20: cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez, once, doce, trece, catorce, quince, dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve, veinte
21–99: veinte uno, treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa
100+: cien (100 alone), ciento uno (101), mil (1000), un millón
Currency: euro (EUR, Spain/EU), peso (Mexico/Latin America), dólar; usar: 'Cuesta... (It costs...)'

example.label: Prices & quantities
example.text: Un café cuesta tres euros. | Estos zapatos cuestan cincuenta y cinco euros. | Necesito cien gramos de jamón.

slides.tip: Practice numbers aloud in real shops—hearing prices in context cements them faster than drills.

slides.title: Asking Directions & Understanding Responses
points: Asking: '¿Dónde está...? (Where is...?)', '¿Cómo llego a...? (How do I get to...?)', '¿Cuál es el camino a...?'
Key directions: izquierda (left), derecha (right), recto/todo recto (straight), atrás (back), adelante (forward)
Locations: cerca de (near), lejos de (far from), al lado de (next to), enfrente de (across from), entre (between)
Responses: 'Gire a la izquierda', 'Siga derecho', 'Está a dos cuadras' (It's two blocks away)

example.label: Getting directions
example.text: — ¿Dónde está la estación de autobuses? | — Está cerca de aquí, a la izquierda. Siga recto por dos cuadras.

slides.tip: Learn 5 local landmarks near your home in Spanish—practice asking how to reach them.

slides.title: Common Phrases & Everyday Courtesies
points: Greetings: Hola, Buenos días, Buenas tardes, Buenas noches, ¿Qué tal? (How's it going?)
Politeness: Por favor (please), Gracias (thanks), De nada (you're welcome), Disculpa/Disculpe (excuse me/pardon)
Responses: Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? | Así así (so-so) | No muy bien (not great)
Small talk: '¿De dónde eres?' (Where are you from?), '¿A qué te dedicas?' (What do you do?), '¿Cuántos años tienes?' (How old are you?)

example.label: Brief conversation
example.text: — Hola, ¿qué tal? | — Muy bien, ¿y tú? | — Bien también. ¿De dónde eres? | — Soy de México. ¿Y tú?

slides.tip: Natives judge fluency partly on natural-sounding phrases—mimic native speakers, not textbooks.

pte-core-overview.title: PTE Core — Canada Immigration & Strategy
pte-core-overview.summary: Navigate PTE Core for Canadian immigration with per-task strategies, CLB mapping, integrated scoring, and realistic timelines.

slides.title: What is PTE Core?
points: PTE Core = Pearson Test of English Core — IRCC-approved test for Canadian immigration (Express Entry, PR applications)
Computer-based, ~2 hours total; measures integrated skills (speaking, reading, writing, listening)
Accepted for: Express Entry (CLB 7+), skilled worker programs, study permit applications
Scores: 10-90 (average: 10 per skill); CLB 7-9 typical immigration targets

slides.title: Test Format at a Glance
points: Speaking (32-39 min): read aloud, repeat sentences, describe images, retell lectures
Integrated Writing (45-50 min): summarize spoken text, write from reading & listening
Reading (29-30 min): multiple choice, fill blanks, reorder paragraphs
Listening (28-32 min): multiple choice, fill blanks, listen & write, highlight incorrect words

slides.title: PTE Core vs. CELPIP (Canada's Top Two)
points: PTE Core: IRCC-approved since 2024, computer-based, integrated tasks, scores in ~3 days, cheaper (~CAD 200)
CELPIP: Canadian brand, human-rated speaking, format: listening, reading, writing, speaking separately, ~CAD 310
Both accepted equally for immigration; PTE is newer, faster, better for non-native pronunciation confidence
Choice: if comfortable with tech, no accent anxiety → PTE; if prefer human raters → CELPIP

slides.title: PTE Core Scoring & CLB Mapping
points: PTE 10-90 converts directly to CLB 2-9 (rough: PTE 10-20=CLB 2, PTE 30-40=CLB 5, PTE 60-70=CLB 8, PTE 80-90=CLB 9)
Express Entry minimum: CLB 7 in English (PTE ~55-60 per skill) or CLB 5-7 in French
Each skill scored separately: Speaking, Reading, Writing, Listening — all must meet target CLB
Integrated tasks: one answer = multiple skills scored (e.g., 'summarize spoken text' = listening + writing)

slides.title: Speaking Tasks: Read Aloud
points: Task: read short texts (20-60 words) aloud within time limit (30-60 sec per text)
Scored on: fluency, pronunciation, intonation — NOT content accuracy
Strategy: read silently first (10 sec), identify stress patterns, hard words; then speak naturally at conversational pace
Common errors: rushing (AI penalizes clipped vowels), pausing mid-word (sounds unnatural), stressing wrong syllable

slides.title: Speaking Tasks: Repeat Sentence
points: Task: listen once, then repeat exactly (word-for-word) in 10-15 sec
Scored on: listening comprehension + accurate repetition + pronunciation
Challenge: no writing allowed — must hold in working memory; some sentences are 20+ words
Strategy: focus on first 3-5 words and rhythm; if you miss a word, don't backtrack, keep fluency; AI reconstructs partial repeats

slides.title: Speaking Tasks: Describe Image
points: Task: see a graph/photo, speak for 25-40 sec describing what you see and trends
Scored on: vocabulary, fluency, grammar, ability to extract and describe data
Format: usually business/science images (graphs, charts, diagrams) — no opinion required, just observation
Strategy: 'I can see... there are... the trend shows... in comparison...' — use linear, descriptive language

slides.title: Speaking Tasks: Retell Lecture
points: Task: listen to 60-90 sec academic lecture, then retell in 40 sec
Scored on: listening accuracy + speaking fluency + capturing key points (not word-for-word)
Lectures are: science, history, business, social studies — spoken once, no subtitles
Strategy: take rough notes (key terms, numbers, names), focus on: 'The lecture discusses... First... Next... Finally...'

slides.title: Integrated Writing: Summarize Spoken Text
points: Task: listen to 60-90 sec recording, write 50-70 word summary in 10 min
Scored on: listening comprehension + writing grammar + capturing main ideas
Note: NOT verbatim transcription — paraphrase in your own words, must identify 3-4 key ideas
Strategy: listen actively, jot keywords, draft quickly, proofread for grammar/spelling in final 2 min

slides.title: Integrated Writing: Write from Reading & Listening
points: Task: read passage (300-400 words), listen to lecture (60-90 sec) on related topic, write 200-300 word response integrating both
Prompt example: 'The passage argues X. The lecture discusses Y. How do they relate?'
Scored on: reading comprehension + listening + writing (grammar, coherence, synthesis)
Strategy: read passage first, take notes; listen and connect ideas; outline: intro (both sources) → comparison → conclusion

slides.title: Reading: Multiple Choice & Reorder Paragraphs
points: Multiple choice (1-2 q): choose best answer based on passage meaning
Reorder paragraphs: put 4-5 scrambled sentences/paragraphs in logical order (~5-10 min)
Scored on: understanding main ideas, discourse coherence, logical flow
Strategy: MC → skim passage for topic sentence; Reorder → look for transition words ('however,' 'furthermore,' 'therefore')

slides.title: Listening: Multiple Choice & Fill Blanks
points: Multiple choice: listen to 30-60 sec clip, answer questions (1 chance only, no replay)
Fill blanks: listen and type missing words in sentences (auto-complete offers suggestions)
Scored on: listening accuracy, vocabulary recognition, audio clarity handling (all recordings are native, clear quality)
Strategy: predict answers (read question first), listen actively, don't overthink fill-blanks (first instinct usually right)

slides.title: Listening: Highlight Incorrect Words
points: Task: read transcript of 30-40 sec recording, mark words that are spoken DIFFERENTLY than written
Example: text says 'colour,' speaker says 'color' → mark it
Challenge: speaker may emphasize, elide, or replace words; requires close attention
Strategy: listen once fully, then go sentence-by-sentence; mark only clear mismatches, not accent/intonation

slides.title: Time Management: The Real Game
points: Speaking (on-the-spot, non-recoverable): 32-39 min → practice pacing until natural
Writing: 45-50 min for 2-3 tasks → spend 15 min per task, 5 min review (don't overwrite, AI penalizes long edits)
Reading: 29-30 min for 3-4 qs → 5-7 min per Q; reading & multiple choice = skimming, reorder = careful reading
Listening: 28-32 min listening + Q time → you can't pause; focus entirely for full segment, then answer immediately

slides.title: Integrated Scoring: One Answer, Multiple Skills
points: 'Summarize spoken text' = Listening (did you understand?) + Writing (grammar, structure, clarity)
'Describe image' = Speaking (fluency, pronunciation) + Vocabulary (descriptive range)
'Write from reading & listening' = Reading + Listening + Writing (synthesis is the highest-order skill)
Key insight: you can't isolate practice — every task practices 2+ skills, so drilling one benefits all

slides.title: Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them
points: Read aloud: speaking too fast or too slow, not breathing naturally (sounds robotic) → record yourself, match native pace
Repeat sentence: forgetting words midway, trying to sound 'perfect' instead of fluent → focus on first words, let fluency carry you
Writing: grammar errors, under-word-count, not synthesizing in integrated tasks → proofread every written answer, always hit minimums
Listening: not predicting before clip, trying to transcribe perfectly → predict question answers, listen for IDEAS not words

slides.title: Preparation Timeline (CLB 7 Target)
points: Week 1-2: understand format, take official practice test (PTE official website), identify weak skill
Week 3-4: drill weak skill daily (if speaking → read aloud 20 times, repeat sentences 30 times)
Week 5-6: full practice tests every 2-3 days, review errors, focus on timing
Week 7-8: final drills, mock tests, confidence-building → ready for test

slides.title: Immigration Next Steps After PTE
points: CLB 7+ (PTE 55+): submit Express Entry (CRS points calculator: age, education, work experience, CLB level)
CRS score 500-600: typical Canadian draws; higher English = higher CRS (every CLB level = ~15 points)
From test to PR: submit, draw issued, get ITA (Invitation to Apply), 60-day deadline for full application, IRCC decision ~6 months
Plan B: if CLB 7 borderline, retake PTE (prep 4-6 weeks, aim CLB 8/9 for safer draw), or explore other pathways (job offer, provincial programs)

slides.title: Pre-Test Checklist (Test Day)
points: Hardware: test in quiet room, headphones/speakers tested, microphone loud and clear, camera angle shows face (proctoring)
Comfort: light meal 2 hours before, water bottle nearby, bathroom break 15 min before (no breaks during test)
Mental: mock test day before to lock in pacing, sleep 8 hours, no new materials on test day
Early arrival: arrive 30 min early if in-center; online: log in 15 min early, run system check twice

slides.title: Scoring & CLB Mapping
points: PTE Core score range: 10–90 Global Scale of English
CLB (Canadian Language Benchmark) mapping: 60+ = CLB 8 (C1), 51–59 = CLB 7 (B2), 40–50 = CLB 6 (B1), below 40 = CLB 5 or lower
Canada immigration (Express Entry, PR): typically requires CLB 7 (PTE 51+) for skilled worker, CLB 9 for management roles
Scores valid for 3 years; tests offered year-round with results in 48 hours

example.label: Score to CLB equivalence
example.text: PTE 60 = CLB 8 (eligible for Express Entry) | PTE 51 = CLB 7 (baseline for most PR streams) | PTE 79 = CLB 9 (advanced professional)

slides.tip: Clarify which CLB level your visa stream requires BEFORE taking the exam—avoids retakes.

slides.title: Speaking Section: Task Types & Scoring
points: 4 speaking tasks: Personal introduction (1 min), Read aloud (8 clips, 40–60 sec each), Repeat sentence (10 clips, 3–9 sec), Speak about image (6 images, 1–2 min each)
AI scoring: fluency (no long pauses), pronunciation (intelligibility, not accent), content (addressing the prompt), grammar & lexis
Total speaking time: ~25–30 min; no human raters, instant scoring
Common failures: reading aloud too fast/stumbling, repeating with missing words, not completing image descriptions

example.label: Repeat sentence task
example.text: You hear: 'The transportation system in modern cities relies heavily on digital infrastructure.' You repeat it clearly, matching pace and stress.

slides.tip: Fluency beats perfection—a natural-sounding sentence with minor grammar beats hesitant, hyper-correct speech.

slides.title: Writing Section: Task Types & Scoring
points: 2 writing tasks: Write email (1 email, 100–150 words, 10 min) and Write essay (1 essay, 200–300 words, 20 min)
Scoring: grammar (tense, agreement), vocabulary (range & accuracy), spelling, punctuation, task completion (all points addressed)
Common errors: run-on sentences, repetitive words, not organizing into paragraphs, missing required tone (formal email vs. casual)

example.label: Email task prompt
example.text: Your colleague sent you a confusing report. Write an email asking for clarification on three specific points. (Tone: polite/professional)

slides.tip: Use templates—a clear email format (greeting, body with 3–4 points, closing) saves time and reduces grammar errors.

slides.title: Listening Section: Task Types & Duration
points: 5 listening tasks: Listen & select (5 questions, 20–30 sec clips), Highlight correct words (1–3 clips, 30–90 sec each), Select missing words (4 clips, 15–30 sec), Fill in blanks (1 passage, 60–90 sec), Transcribe (1 clip, 30–90 sec)
Total listening time: ~20 min; mixed accents (British, North American, Australian), realistic speech (natural pace, colloquialisms)
Scoring: content accuracy, not transcription perfection for most tasks except 'Transcribe'
Challenge: background noise, speakers interrupting, colloquial expressions

example.label: Listen & select task
example.text: You hear a 25-second conversation; choose the answer: 'What is the main topic?' (A) budget cuts (B) office relocation (C) recruitment.

slides.tip: Train your ear with diverse accents early—PTE uses unscripted, natural speech, not textbook English.

slides.title: Reading Section: Task Types & Time Management
points: 4 reading tasks: Multiple choice (3–5 questions), Reorder paragraphs (1 passage, 5–7 sentences), Fill blanks (3–4 passages, 4–5 blanks each), Match headings (one long passage, 4–6 paragraphs)
Total reading time: ~30 min; mix of academic and general topics; vocabulary level B1–B2
Scoring: accuracy only—no partial credit; one wrong answer = zero for that question
Time trap: 'Match headings' can eat 10 min if you don't skim first

example.label: Match headings task
example.text: Read 5 paragraphs on climate change; match each to a heading (A) emission sources (B) mitigation strategies (C) economic impact, etc. Each heading used only once.

slides.tip: Read the heading set FIRST, then skim each paragraph for the main idea—saves time vs. reading paragraphs first.

slides.title: PTE Core vs. PTE Academic: Key Differences
points: PTE Core: designed for Canadian immigration (Express Entry, provincial nominees), CLB-aligned, 3 hours total, no writing/reading at upper-advanced level
PTE Academic: international test (US, UK, Australia), CEFR-aligned (C1–C2), 3 hours, academic/professional content
Content difference: Core uses everyday scenarios (workplace, community); Academic uses research papers, complex arguments
Difficulty: Core B2 level average; Academic C1+ level average; Core is typically easier for non-native speakers targeting PR

example.label: Content comparison
example.text: Core writing prompt: 'Email your manager about a project delay.' | Academic prompt: 'Analyze the sociological impact of remote work on organizational culture.'

slides.tip: Choose Core if immigrating to Canada; choose Academic if applying to universities or professional roles outside Canada.

cambridge-overview.title: Cambridge English — B2 First & C1 Advanced Strategy
cambridge-overview.summary: Master Cambridge B2 First and C1 Advanced with per-paper tactics, traps to avoid, level selection guide, and progression pathways.

slides.title: Welcome to Cambridge English
points: Cambridge English (University of Cambridge): oldest, most respected English qualifications worldwide (since 1913)
Two exam targets: B2 First (formerly FCE) = upper-intermediate, C1 Advanced (formerly CAE) = advanced
Global recognition: universities (60+ countries), employers, immigration (UK Visa & Immigration accepts both)
Cambridge Scale: 140-230 (B2 First: 160-179, C1 Advanced: 180+); aligned with CEFR levels

slides.title: B2 First vs. C1 Advanced: Which Should You Take?
points: B2 First: upper-intermediate English, can understand complex texts, express opinions, write formal emails
C1 Advanced: advanced fluency, near-native, subtle argumentation, nuanced writing, specialized vocabulary
Career/study path: B2 = job entry (nursing, teaching, tech), C1 = leadership roles, academic research, advanced negotiations
Rule of thumb: if IELTS 6.5-7.0 → B2 First; IELTS 7.5-8.0 → C1 Advanced; unsure? take B2 first, upgrade if strong

slides.title: Cambridge Scale & Score Mapping
points: Cambridge Scale: 140-230 (70 points = one CEFR level)
B2 First: 160-179 (lower band) to (upper band); C1 Advanced: 180-199 (lower) to 200-230 (upper)
Pass criteria: B2 requires ~60% (160/230 score threshold varies by test session)
Score calculation: 5 papers weighted equally (Reading, Writing, Listening, Speaking, Use of English) → average = final score

slides.title: Paper 1: Reading & Use of English (90 minutes)
points: Part 1 (Multiple choice, 8 qs): vocabulary in context, read short texts, choose best word
Part 2 (Cloze, 8 qs): fill 8 blanks in passage with given words, tests grammar/collocation
Part 3 (Word formation, 10 qs): fill blanks with correct form of word (e.g., clear → clearly, clarity, unclear)
Part 4 (Key word transformation, 6 qs): rewrite sentence with given word, keep meaning (e.g., 'She's allergic to peanuts' → 'If she eats peanuts, she...')

slides.title: Reading Strategy & Common Traps
points: Part 1 (vocabulary): distractor = synonym that doesn't fit context; read entire sentence, not just blank
Part 2 (cloze): word order, prepositions, articles matter; if unsure, read surrounding sentences for grammar clues
Part 3 (word formation): read suffix rules; -tion, -ment, -ly, -ness are high-frequency; watch negative prefixes (un-, dis-, in-)
Part 4 (key word): rephrase meaning without changing structure; if given 'despite,' rewrite the negative → 'Although not/Although... not'

slides.title: Paper 2: Writing (90 minutes, 2 tasks)
points: Part 1 (Compulsory): email, letter, proposal, or report — ~150 words, formal/neutral register
Part 2 (Choice of 4): article, email, essay, review, story, or proposal — ~250 words, register depends on prompt
Scored on: task achievement (did you answer the prompt?), organization, language range, grammar accuracy
Time: 35-40 min Part 1, 50-55 min Part 2; leave 5 min to proofread both

slides.title: Writing: Register & Tone
points: Formal (email, letter, proposal, report): no contractions ('I'm' → 'I am'), no slang, complex sentences, passive voice for politeness
Neutral (article, essay): standard English, clear structure, cite examples, balanced tone
Informal (review, story): contractions OK, personal voice, emotion, dynamic verbs
Trap: mixing registers (using 'Hi' in formal email, or 'Thus' in casual review) = marks lost; identify register from prompt first

slides.title: Paper 3: Listening (40 minutes, ~30 qs)
points: Part 1 (8 short audio clips, 8 MCQ): everyday conversations, choose best answer (3 options each)
Part 2 (longer monologue, 10 fill-blanks): write 1-3 words per blank, spelling matters
Part 3 (conversation, 5 MCQ or matching): longer exchange, nuanced meaning, inference required
Part 4 (multiple speakers, 7 matching): match 5-7 statements to correct speaker — requires close listening to tone, opinion

slides.title: Listening Strategy & Common Traps
points: Part 1: answer choices are close synonyms; listen for specific detail, not general meaning
Part 2 (fill blanks): exact spelling required; if you hear 'accommodation,' spell it correctly or lose mark
Part 3: intonation matters — sarcasm, stress, hesitation change meaning; speaker may express doubts ('kind of,' 'I suppose')
Part 4: match OPINION not topic; if speaker says 'Films are important but books are better,' they prefer books, not films

slides.title: Paper 4: Speaking (14-17 minutes, 4 parts)
points: Part 1 (2 min): interview about yourself, family, work, interests — assessor asks 5-6 questions
Part 2 (4 min): describe a photo (1 min), then partner describes theirs, discuss similarities/differences (3 min)
Part 3 (4 min): collaborative task — given topic/problem, discuss and reach agreement with partner
Part 4 (3-4 min): abstract questions on Part 3 topic, e.g., 'How important is technology in modern life?'

slides.title: Speaking: Performance Tips
points: Part 1: give full answers (not yes/no), use present tense, extend with examples ('I enjoy reading... particularly fiction')
Part 2: allocate time—photo description 1 min (use 'The photo shows... In the background... The person appears to...'), comparison 2.5 min
Part 3: agree/disagree tactfully ('I see your point, but... I'd add that...'), use conditionals ('If we implemented X, then Y might happen')
Part 4: connect to general themes, use sophisticated vocabulary ('paradoxically,' 'conversely,' 'arguably'), pause naturally (not robotic)

slides.title: Common Speaking Mistakes
points: Memorized answers: assessor hears rehearsed responses → marks down for lack of engagement; speak spontaneously
Talking too much in Part 1: keep answers 20-30 sec; extended monologues bore assessors
Ignoring partner in Part 3: if you dominate, you lose interaction marks; listen and respond to their ideas
Grammatical avoidance: using only simple sentences to 'play it safe' → aim for complex + some risk (even if imperfect) = higher marks

slides.title: C1 Advanced: Key Differences from B2 First
points: Reading & Use of English: narrower time (90 min same as B2), but higher density of complex vocabulary, subtle inference, academic register
Writing: expect more sophisticated task (e.g., essay with nuanced position, review of academic paper), wider range of register required
Listening: faster pace, more accents (regional UK, Irish, Australian English), abstract topics, subtle tone/opinion differences
Speaking: C1 assessor scores on fluency, sophistication, accuracy; B2 scores on accuracy, range, fluency — C1 expects near-native spontaneity

slides.title: Time Management Across Papers
points: Reading & Use of English: Part 1 (12 min), Part 2 (15 min), Part 3 (20 min), Part 4 (18 min), Part 5 (25 min) = 90 min balanced
Writing: Part 1 (40 min), Part 2 (50 min) = 90 min; don't spend 60 min on Part 1 or you'll rush Part 2
Listening: passive listening only — no pausing, no control; follow pace; leave 1-2 min at end to review answers (if you haven't been writing)
Speaking: assessor controls timing; don't interrupt, let them finish questions; use pauses naturally (not long silence, but 2-3 sec OK)

slides.title: Top 5 Test-Day Traps & How to Avoid Them
points: Running out of time on Writing Part 2: leave 50 min for Part 2 even if Part 1 feels incomplete; incomplete Part 1 = fewer marks, no Part 2 = zero marks
Forgetting to proofread: grammar/spelling errors = marks lost; 5 min proofread on Writing catches ~30% of errors
Misreading Part 4 (key word) instructions: some tests ask 'Write 3-6 words,' others 'Write 2-5 words' — read instruction first
Mispronouncing words in Speaking: if unsure, say it confidently (mumbling = incomprehensibility mark loss); 'tomato' accent OK if clear
Not signposting ideas in Writing: use transitions ('Furthermore,' 'However,' 'To illustrate'); examiners penalize unclear paragraph flow

slides.title: Preparation Timeline: B2 First (6-8 weeks)
points: Week 1: diagnostic test (official Cambridge mock), identify weak paper (most lose marks in Reading Part 4 or Writing)
Week 2-3: drill weak paper daily (Part 4 = 30 min on 'key word' practice, Writing = write mini-essays every 2 days)
Week 4-5: full reading & writing papers, listening/speaking with tutor, focus on time limits
Week 6-7: 2-3 full practice tests, review every error, adjust strategy (if Part 4 still weak, do 50 transformations extra)
Week 8: final confidence drills, no new materials, rest 2 days before test

slides.title: Preparation Timeline: C1 Advanced (10-12 weeks)
points: Week 1-2: diagnostic test, understand C1 vocabulary depth (academic, abstract, nuanced meaning)
Week 3-5: vocabulary building (C1 word lists, etymology, collocations), drilling Reading Part 5 (dense passages, inference)
Week 6-7: Writing Part 1 (formal synthesis of multiple sources), Part 2 (argumentative essay with counterargument)
Week 8-9: Listening (diverse accents, abstract topics), Speaking (fluency without hesitation, sophisticated opinion)
Week 10-11: 3+ full practice tests, review for error patterns, fine-tune weak skills
Week 12: rest, confidence only, sleep well

slides.title: After Cambridge: Next Steps & Careers
points: B2 First: nursing (UK/Australia/Canada), teaching English abroad, tech support roles, EU job migration, university entry (non-Anglophone countries)
C1 Advanced: university postgraduate study, professional services (law, consulting), academic research, international leadership roles
Maintaining score: Cambridge certs are valid forever, but if 5+ years have passed and job requires proof of 'current' English, IELTS/TOEFL annual retake safer
Plan: B2 First (6-12 months of study) → start working/studying in English environment → upgrade to C1 in 1-2 years if career growth demands it

slides.title: Final Exam Tips & Confidence Boosters
points: On test day: arrive 30 min early, eat light breakfast (stable blood sugar), 30-min light review only (not new materials)
During test: mark answers confidently, don't second-guess Part 1 answers after 2 sec thought; trust instinct
Speaking: smile (assessor hears it), make eye contact, show enthusiasm; you're being scored on confidence + accuracy
After test: don't obsess over 'did I get Q12 right?' — move forward; results come in 2-3 weeks; if you fail, retaking is common and builds resilience

slides.title: Cambridge Levels & CEFR Alignment
points: Cambridge exams map to Common European Framework (CEFR): A1–C2 scale
A1–A2: KET (Key English Test), qualifying exam
B1–B2: PET (Preliminary), FCE (First Certificate in English)
C1–C2: CAE (Certificate in Advanced English), CPE (Certificate of Proficiency in English)
UK requires B1 for university admission; B2 for professional migration (some fields require C1)

example.label: CEFR level requirements
example.text: A2 = survival basics | B1 = workplace communication | B2 = professional fluency | C1 = academic research | C2 = native-like mastery

slides.tip: Research your target country's requirement BEFORE signing up—B2 is the 'safe zone' for most UK/EU opportunities.

slides.title: Paper Structure: Reading, Writing, Listening, Speaking
points: Reading (1 hr 15 min): 52 questions across 8 texts; mix of articles, emails, adverts, extracted passages
Writing (1 hr 20 min): 2 tasks—'For and against essay' (250 words) and 'Letter/email' (140–190 words)
Listening (40 min): 4 sections with 30 questions; monologues, conversations, lectures; British English accent
Speaking (14 min per pair): conversational interview, topic discussion, collaborative task with partner, individual long turn

example.label: Reading section sample
example.text: Text 1: Magazine article (6–8 multiple-choice questions) | Text 2: Email exchange (5–6 gap-fill) | Text 3: Website content (8–10 matching headings)

slides.tip: Speaking is done with a partner OR in groups—practice with a conversation buddy; don't panic if unfamiliar faces join.

slides.title: Scoring, Grades & Pass Bands
points: Scoring: raw marks converted to scaled scores (0–200 for B2/C1); grade boundaries vary by exam date
Pass grades: A (highest), B (pass), C (pass); D/E = fail
Minimum 60% overall to pass; uneven performance (one section weak) can pull down grade despite other sections excelling
Cambridge Certificate valid indefinitely; no score decay; employers/universities verify online

example.label: Grade thresholds (approx)
example.text: FCE: 180–199 = Grade A | 160–179 = Grade B | 140–159 = Grade C | 120–139 = Fail

slides.tip: Aim for balanced scores across sections—one section at 50% drags down the overall grade even if others are 85%.

slides.title: Cambridge vs. IELTS: Strengths & Differences
points: Cambridge: British English focus, more academic/formal texts, speaking with examiner (not panel), international recognition steady but IELTS more known globally
IELTS: Australian/American/British mix, more real-world scenarios (news, job adverts), larger test centers worldwide, scores valid 2 years only
Writing: Cambridge essays more formal & structured; IELTS allows more varied tone (Task 2 can be argumentative/analytical/advisory)
Difficulty perception: Cambridge B2 (FCE) ≈ IELTS 6.5–7 | Cambridge C1 (CAE) ≈ IELTS 7.5–8

example.label: Writing prompt difference
example.text: Cambridge: 'Do you agree or disagree: Remote work reduces team cohesion?' | IELTS: 'Some argue remote work harms office culture. Discuss.'

slides.tip: Choose Cambridge if you want to study in the UK or settle there long-term; IELTS if you want maximum global portability.

slides.title: Who Accepts Cambridge: Universities, Employers, Migration
points: UK universities: almost all accept B2 (FCE) or C1 (CAE); some elite programs require C1
US universities: less common than TOEFL/IELTS; some accept Cambridge but verify with admissions first
Employers: major corporates (KPMG, Shell, HSBC) recognize Cambridge C1 as proof of professional English
Visa/Migration: UK Visas accept B1+ (PET) for spouse visa, C1 (CAE) for Tier 2 work visas; Australia/Canada prefer IELTS

example.label: Typical acceptance
example.text: Oxford/Cambridge: B2/C1 minimum | British Airways cabin crew: C1 | UK Spouse Visa: B1 | Professional registration (engineering UK): B2

slides.tip: Verify your specific institution/employer BEFORE taking Cambridge—not all fields equally recognize it globally.

slides.title: Preparation Tips: Strengths to Exploit, Common Pitfalls to Avoid
points: Exploit: Cambridge material is authentic (real articles, emails); immerse in British media (BBC, The Guardian, podcasts). Partner speaking practice—less intimidating than solo.
Pitfalls: speaking nerves spike when paired with stranger—normalize it. Writing essays are formulaic; avoid robotic templates. Reading: time pressure is real—speed-read headings/skimming first.
3–4 month prep standard; B2 faster than C1; practice tests 2–3 weeks before exam (confidence booster). Take a mock with official conditions.

example.label: Balanced prep week
example.text: Mon–Wed: 1 section/day (reading, writing, listening) | Thu: speaking practice with partner | Fri–Sat: mixed practice under timed conditions | Sun: review weak areas

slides.tip: Join a Cambridge prep group (online or local)—peer feedback on speaking/writing beats solo study.

cael-overview.title: CAEL — Canadian Academic English Language Test
cael-overview.summary: Master CAEL for Canadian university admission with integrated task strategies, CLB mapping, academic vocabulary, and realistic prep timelines.

slides.title: What is CAEL?
points: CAEL = Canadian Academic English Language Test — assesses academic English for Canadian university/college admission
Integrated test: tasks combine reading + listening + writing + speaking in real academic scenarios (mimics university classroom)
Accepted by: 300+ Canadian institutions (U of T, McGill, UBC, McMaster, etc.), some US universities, Australian universities
Score: 10-90 (CLB 4-9 mapping); universities typically require CLB 6-8 (CAEL 50-80) for admission

slides.title: CAEL vs. IELTS & TOEFL: Why Choose CAEL?
points: CAEL is integrated (academic simulation); IELTS/TOEFL are modular (skills separated by paper)
CAEL favors: students confident in real-world academic English, Canadian university preparation, CLB-to-CAEL direct admission pathways
IELTS/TOEFL: broader global acceptance, more practice materials available, longer test history (more familiar to institutions)
Strategic choice: if targeting Canadian universities → CAEL (recognized by admissions offices directly); if unsure about destination → IELTS (safe global choice)

slides.title: CAEL Scoring & CLB Mapping
points: University admission benchmarks: CLB 6 (50) = conditional entry (English support class required), CLB 7 (65) = direct admission, CLB 8+ (75+) = competitive for grad school
Score validity: 2 years from test date; after 2 years, universities may request re-testing
Registration: CAEL offered year-round online; test results in 2-3 weeks

slides.title: CAEL Test Format (90 minutes, 4 integrated tasks)
points: Task 1 (Reading → Speaking): read academic text (300-400 words), then speak opinion/summary (2-3 min response)
Task 2 (Listening → Writing): watch/listen to academic lecture (3-5 min), write summary + analysis (200-250 words, 15 min write time)
Task 3 (Reading + Listening → Writing): read text, listen to lecture on related topic, write comparison/synthesis (250-300 words, 20 min)
Task 4 (Listening → Speaking): listen to conversation or debate, then discuss with AI (speaking, 2-3 min)

slides.title: Task 1: Reading & Speaking (20 minutes)
points: Read: 300-400 word academic text on social sciences, science, or business topic; you have ~10 min to read
Speak: express your opinion/analysis on a question about the text (e.g., 'Do you agree with the author's argument about climate change?')
Scored on: listening (did you understand the text?), speaking fluency, grammar, vocabulary range
Strategy: read first, underline 2-3 key ideas, form opinion; speak for full 2-3 min with examples from text + your knowledge

slides.title: Task 2: Listening & Writing (25 minutes)
points: Listen: academic lecture (3-5 min) on university-level topic — you can take notes (note-taking paper provided)
Write: summarize main ideas + analyze (200-250 words); questions like 'What were the main arguments? How does this support/contradict X?'
Scored on: listening comprehension (did you capture key ideas?), writing organization, grammar, vocabulary
Challenge: lecture is played once only; no replay or transcript; must take rapid notes and synthesize while writing

slides.title: Task 2: Note-Taking Strategies
points: Listen for: signposting ('There are 3 main points...'), stressed words, transitions ('However,' 'Furthermore'), repetition (speaker emphasizes = important)
Note efficiently: abbreviations (govt = government, exp = example, vs = versus), symbols (→ = leads to, ↑ = increases), fragments not full sentences
During writing: check notes for 3+ main ideas, draft topic sentence, quote 1 short phrase from lecture if possible, analyze briefly, conclude

Example: Lecture on 'renewable energy barriers.' Notes: 1) cost (solar expensive upfront), 2) grid infrastructure (old systems can't adapt), 3) policy (subsidies slow). Write: synthesize all three, don't over-quote

slides.title: Task 3: Reading + Listening & Writing (30 minutes)
points: Read: academic text (250-350 words) on Topic A — 10 min to read and note
Listen: related lecture (3-4 min) on Topic B (contrasting or expanding on Text) — take notes
Write: synthesis (250-300 words) answering 'How do these sources relate? Agree? Disagree? What does this reveal?'
Scored on: comprehension of both sources, synthesis (connecting ideas), writing quality, critical thinking

slides.title: Task 3: Synthesis Writing Strategy
points: Outline (3 min): intro (both sources + your thesis), body (point 1 both agree on, point 2 they differ, point 3 implication), conclusion
Intro formula: 'Source A argues X. The lecture presents Y. Together, they suggest Z.'
Body: use transitions ('While X claims... the lecture counters...'), cite each source ('According to the text...' / 'The speaker mentioned...')
Avoid: merely summarizing each source separately; instead, interweave: 'The text states X because of Y, but the lecture challenges this by noting Z.'
Word count: 250-300 words = ~5 min intro + 10 min body + 2 min conclusion; write first draft fast, proofread in final 3 min

slides.title: Task 4: Listening & Speaking (15 minutes)
points: Listen: recorded conversation or debate (2-3 min) between 2-3 speakers on academic topic; you take mental notes
Respond: AI or interviewer asks: 'What are the speakers' positions? Which do you find more convincing? Why?'
Scored on: listening understanding, speaking fluency, coherence, vocabulary, ability to synthesize differing views
Challenge: no notes allowed; you must hold ideas in memory while speaking; pressure to respond immediately

slides.title: Task 4: Listening & Speaking Tips
points: During listen: try to identify 2-3 speakers and their main positions (e.g., 'Speaker A pro-X, Speaker B pro-Y')
Speaking formula: 'Speaker A believes... because... Speaker B counters by... I find A's argument more convincing because...'
Extend: 'If we consider X and Y, then the implications are... In my experience/view...'
Pacing: speak for 2-3 min naturally; don't rush or pause awkwardly; if you lose a detail, move forward (don't backtrack asking 'wait, what did they say?')

slides.title: Academic Vocabulary for CAEL Success
points: High-frequency: argue, claim, evidence, analysis, support, contradict, imply, conclude, research, methodology, significant, relevant, implications
Advanced: counterargument, substantiate, leverage, inhibit, facilitate, paradoxically, conversely, synthesis, coherence, pragmatic
Collocation patterns: 'strong evidence,' 'key argument,' 'critical analysis,' 'research methodology,' 'policy implications'
Vocab building: use Anki flashcards (academic CAEL deck), read academic journal summaries, listen to TED talks, practice synonym replacement

slides.title: Time Management During CAEL (90 total minutes)
points: Task 1 (20 min): 10 read, 2-3 speak + 5 min buffer if you need to reread
Task 2 (25 min): 5 listen, 15 write (includes 2 min proofread), 5 min buffer
Task 3 (30 min): 10 read + listen, 20 write = 5 min outline, 12 min draft, 3 min proofread
Task 4 (15 min): 3 listen, 2-3 speak, rest = admin/instructions
Buffer: built-in cushion; if you finish early, use extra time to proofread writing tasks only (don't change content, just fix errors)

slides.title: Common CAEL Mistakes & How to Avoid Them
points: Task 1: memorizing a generic opinion, not engaging with the text → always reference text details ('The author says X, and I agree because...')
Task 2: missing main idea by focusing on examples → listen for signposting first ('Today I'll discuss 3 main points...'), then examples support those
Task 3: summarizing each source separately instead of synthesizing → use compare-contrast language from day 1 ('Similarly, both...'; 'In contrast...')
Task 4: panicking if you miss a word → don't apologize or ask to replay; speak to what you understood ('One speaker mentioned X, which is important because...')

slides.title: Preparation Timeline: CAEL (8-10 weeks)
points: Week 1: diagnostic CAEL practice test, identify weak task (often Task 3 synthesis = most challenging)
Week 2-3: vocabulary building (academic word list), Task 1-2 practice separately (2-3 times each)
Week 4-5: Task 3 focus (synthesis writing drills 3x per week, full task 2x), start note-taking training
Week 6-7: Task 4 (speaking practice with partner/tutor), full integrated simulations (all 4 tasks in 90 min)
Week 8-9: 2-3 full practice tests, review errors, final vocabulary review
Week 10: light practice only, rest, confidence-building

slides.title: Resources for CAEL Study
points: Official: CAEL.ca (practice tests, sample answers, scoring rubrics), CAEL YouTube channel (example tasks)
Materials: 'CAEL Preparation Guide' (free from test center), academic reading lists (CAEL website provides sample texts)
Note-taking: Cornell notes method or mind-mapping for lectures; practice with TED talks / YouTube academic videos
Speaking: record yourself for Task 1 & 4; listen for pacing, grammar, vocabulary range; adjust if too formal or too casual

slides.title: CAEL for Canadian University Admission
points: Bachelor's programs: CLB 6 (CAEL 50) typical requirement; CLB 7+ (CAEL 65+) competitive for top programs
Master's programs: CLB 7-8 (CAEL 65-80) required; some research-heavy programs may want CLB 8+ (CAEL 80+)
Conditional admission: CLB 5 (CAEL 35-40) → offered admission BUT must complete English 100-level support course first semester
Application timeline: submit CAEL with application (Oct-Dec for Jan entry, Dec-Mar for Sept entry); early submission = better scholarship eligibility

slides.title: Pre-Test Checklist & Test Day
points: Equipment: computer with working webcam/microphone, headphones, stable internet (test-run 24 hours before)
Environment: quiet room, no distractions, notepad + pencil on desk for Task 2 note-taking
Preparation: light breakfast, 20-min warm-up speaking in English (5 min reading aloud + 5 min speaking opinion on random topic)
During test: follow all instructions, don't skip tasks, speak clearly into microphone, type all writing fully (incomplete = zero marks)

slides.title: After CAEL: Next Steps
points: Score CLB 6+: submit to universities for admission, register for courses, apply for student visa if needed
Score CLB 5 or below: prepare retake plan (4-6 weeks, drill weak task), consult with test center on scheduling
Accepted to university: begin ESL/English support class if conditional (don't skip — helps transition to full course load)
Career pathway: bachelor's in Canada → work permit → PR → many international students become permanent residents within 3 years of graduation

slides.title: CAEL Section Breakdown & Task Types
points: Listening (30 min): 2 lectures, 10 questions each (note-taking, gist, specific detail); realistic classroom pace
Reading (50 min): 3 academic passages, 10 questions each (main idea, inference, vocabulary, detail); B1–B2 level
Writing (60 min): 2 tasks—integrate source + personal view (250 words) and respond to a statement (250 words)
Speaking (15 min): monologue on prompt, conversation with examiner on academic topic; no separate 'fluency round'

example.label: Writing task example
example.text: Read a passage on climate policy. Summarize 2 key points + explain your own perspective (agree/disagree with one). 250 words, 30 min.

slides.tip: CAEL writing is integration-heavy—practice synthesizing source material into your own argument.

slides.title: Scoring System & Passing Score
points: Scoring: 0–9 scale per section; overall band is the average of 4 sections (reported as 0–9 band, e.g., 6.5 = B1 level)
Passing score varies by institution: most Canadian universities require 5.0–5.5 (B1), some professional programs require 6.0+ (B1–B2)
Minimum requirement: no section below 4.0 at most universities (rules out 'compensating' with one strong section)
Results valid for 2 years; cheaper than IELTS/TOEFL (CAD $340 vs. $300+)

example.label: Band score interpretation
example.text: CAEL 5.0 = B1 intermediate (understood by Canadians, handles academic tasks) | CAEL 7.0 = B2–C1 (strong academic reading, near-native speaking)

slides.tip: Clarify your target institution's minimum—5.0 is standard for most Canadian programs; don't overprepare if 5.5 is needed.

slides.title: Who Accepts CAEL: Canadian Universities & Programs
points: All Canadian universities accept CAEL (designed in Canada, used by 60+ institutions)
Primary users: University of British Columbia, McGill, University of Toronto, University of Alberta, Ryerson, Waterloo
Professional programs: nursing, education, engineering sometimes require 6.0+; business & arts typically 5.0–5.5
NOT widely accepted outside Canada—IELTS/TOEFL better for Australia, UK, US graduate programs

example.label: University requirements
example.text: UBC Master's (STEM): CAEL 5.5 | McGill MBA: CAEL 6.0 | Ryerson Nursing: CAEL 5.5, no section below 4.5

slides.tip: If targeting US or non-Canadian schools, take IELTS instead—CAEL not recognized outside Canada/rare in US.

slides.title: CAEL vs. IELTS vs. TOEFL: Quick Comparison
points: CAEL: Canadian focus, integration-heavy writing, realistic listening (classroom pace). Cost-effective. Easiest for Canadian applicants familiar with Canadian English.
IELTS: Global acceptance, flexible writing (task 1 letter + task 2 essay), British/Australian accents. 2-year validity.
TOEFL: US-centric (accepted in Canada but less common), academic reading/listening complex, computer-based. Priciest.
For Canada: CAEL saves time/money; for Australia/UK/US: IELTS universally accepted.

example.label: Difficulty/prep time comparison
example.text: CAEL writing (integration) easiest if you're already reading sources. | IELTS writing Task 1 (letter format) can be simpler than TOEFL academic essay. | TOEFL listening fastest for multi-accent speakers.

slides.tip: Take a free CAEL practice test—if it feels natural, CAEL saves 2–4 weeks vs. re-prepping for IELTS.

slides.title: Test Format: Computer-Based, Timed, Integrated Tasks
points: Format: entirely computer-based; no paper option (all typing & reading on screen)
Duration: 2 hr 45 min total (listening 30 min, reading 50 min, writing 60 min, speaking 15 min)
Integrated writing: you read + listen + write (synthesis required; not separate tasks like IELTS)
Speaking: monologue + Q&A with examiner (not panel, not interview with strangers—same examiner talks to you one-on-one)

example.label: Integrated writing flow
example.text: You read a passage on automation (5 min) → listen to a lecture discussing it (5 min) → write synthesizing both views (30 min)

slides.tip: Practice integrated writing tasks weeks before—it's a unique skill; IELTS/TOEFL test separate skills.

slides.title: Preparation Strategy: Common Mistakes & Pro Tips
points: Mistake 1: ignoring integration—treating writing as separate summary + opinion. Practice linking sources to your view.
Mistake 2: speaking too fast / not elaborating in monologue. Pause, think, elaborate with examples. Aim for 2–3 min of coherent speech.
Mistake 3: weak listening note-taking—miss details on second listen. Practice Cornell notes (left column: main ideas; right: details).
Pro tip 1: CAEL allows you to SEE reading passages while writing (unlike some tests)—use this advantage. Re-read, cite, integrate.
Pro tip 2: speaking is NOT scored on accent—focus on clarity, grammar, lexical range. Rehearse 2–3 times with recording yourself.

example.label: Strong integrated writing
example.text: Source: 'Automation reduces jobs.' Lecture: 'But creates new skills-based roles.' Your synthesis: 'While automation displaces workers (source 1), evidence suggests new employment emerges (source 2). However, retraining is critical...'

slides.tip: Practice under real exam conditions 2 weeks before—sitting for 2h 45 min is exhausting; build stamina.
